summary: Defines an LDAP schema, meaning object classes and attributes, for describing printers and printer services in a directory. It is based on the printer attributes listed in the Internet Printing Protocol and on the Printer MIB. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 7612.

eli5.summary: A school keeps a phone book of people. This adds a page for printers, with fields like what each can do, so computers can look one up.

how do you store printer information in ldap
can ldap work with service location protocol for printers
subtitle: Directory schema for describing printer devices and their capabilities.

tldr.problem: Organizations use LDAP directories to store information about networked resources, but there was no standard way to describe printers and their capabilities (speeds, colors, paper sizes, supported formats) so applications could discover and select the right printer.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3712 defines LDAP object classes and attributes for storing printer information, based on attributes from Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) and the Printer MIB, allowing any LDAP-enabled application to query printer properties.
tldr.outcome: This schema enables printer discovery and selection in enterprise networks. It was replaced by RFC 7612, which updated the schema for modern printing environments.

facts.label: Internationalization
facts.value: Full support via UTF-8 and language tags

today: RFC 3712 is Informational and was superseded by RFC 7612, which provides updated LDAP schema for printer services. Organizations continue to use LDAP schemas based on these definitions to store printer information, though the exact attributes and object classes may vary based on local needs and implementations.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
This RFC defines LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) schema for printers and printer services. It allows organizations to store and query printer information in their LDAP directory, the same centralized database they use for users, computers, and other network resources.

The schema is based on printer attributes from Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) 1.1 (RFC 2911) and the Printer MIB (RFC 1759). It is technically aligned with the Service Location Protocol (SLP) printer service template, so organizations using SLP service discovery can interwork with LDAP-based discovery.
sections.eli5: Computers and applications can ask the directory "Show me all color printers on the third floor" or "Which printer prints the fastest?". The directory has fields for each printer's capabilities so it can answer these questions.

sections.title: Object Classes for Printers
sections.content:
The schema defines six LDAP object classes, which are templates for creating printer directory entries:

printerService is the main structural class for printer entries. It inherits common attributes from printerAbstract, which defines the base set of all printer-related attributes (like name, location, speed, color support).

printerServiceAuxClass is used when extending entries of other types (for example, a room or a floor) with printer information, without making them full printer entries.

printerIPP and printerLPR are auxiliary classes for adding protocol-specific information. An entry can use printerService together with both printerIPP (for Internet Printing Protocol) and printerLPR (for the older Line Printer daemon protocol) to describe a printer that supports both.

slpServicePrinter is for printers registered with Service Location Protocol (SLP), allowing LDAP and SLP to share the same printer data.
sections.eli5: A printer entry can be a simple printer, or a printer that also supports certain protocols like IPP or LPR. You can add extra information for printers that are listed in both LDAP and SLP directories. The abstract class is the shared template for all printer attributes.

sections.title: Printer Attributes
sections.content:
The schema defines 34 attributes covering printer identification, capabilities, and operational information.

Identification attributes include printer-uri (the network address), printer-name (administrative name), printer-location (physical location like "Room 123A"), printer-info (descriptive text), and printer-make-and-model (manufacturer and model string).

Capability attributes describe what the printer can do: printer-color-supported (boolean), printer-pages-per-minute and printer-pages-per-minute-color (throughput), printer-compression-supported (gzip, deflate, etc.), printer-document-format-supported (MIME types accepted), printer-sides-supported (single or double-sided printing), printer-media-supported (paper sizes and types), printer-resolution-supported (dots per inch), printer-finishings-supported (stapling, binding, hole-punch).

Operational attributes include printer-current-operator (contact for the operator) and printer-service-person (contact for maintenance). These allow users and administrators to reach the right person when needed.

Configuration attributes like printer-natural-language-configured (language for messages) and printer-charset-configured (character encoding) support internationalization.
sections.eli5: The attributes store basic facts: what the printer is called, where it is, what it looks like. Then capability attributes say what it can do: color or not, speed, what paper sizes, what file types. Some attributes list who to call if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Design Choices for Matching and Searching
sections.content:
The RFC explains design decisions for how LDAP searches work on printer attributes. String attributes use caseIgnoreMatch, meaning searches for "Room 123a" match "Room 123A". This is user-friendly for names and descriptions.

URI attributes use case-insensitive matching for the hostname part (following RFC 2396), but this is a compromise: strictly case-sensitive matching could cause false negatives (different capitalization is treated as different URIs), while fully case-insensitive matching could cause false positives in the path portion. Most deployed clients "pretty up" hostnames, so case-insensitive matching for the host part is practical.

Keyword attributes like printer-finishings-supported use case-insensitive matching and can be extended with site-specific names beyond the standard IPP keywords. For example, a site might use 'special-blue-binding' as a custom finishing option.

All string attributes support case-insensitive substring matching, so a search for "laser" finds "LaserJet" printers.
sections.eli5: When you search for "Room 123a", the directory finds "Room 123A" because the search ignores uppercase and lowercase differences. The same works for printer names and other text fields. This is friendlier than forcing users to match capitalization exactly.

sections.title: Use in Directory Services and Printing
sections.content:
This schema is used in LDAP directories within organizations to maintain current information about available printers. Applications and users can query the directory to find a printer matching their needs: 'Show me all duplex color printers that support PostScript and PDF.' Administrators maintain printer information by adding, updating, or removing printer entries in the directory. When a printer is installed, decommissioned, or changes capabilities, the directory entry is updated. This gives all clients a current, centralized view of the printing infrastructure.

The schema's alignment with IPP and SLP allows interoperability: a print discovery application can work with both LDAP and SLP directories, or SLP advertisements can be automatically synced with LDAP entries.
sections.eli5: When you print a document, your computer can ask the directory 'What color printers are near me?' The directory returns a list. Administrators keep the directory up to date by adding new printers and noting when old ones are removed.
